section_summary: This section contains tables and press extracts on Japanese gold exports, gold production, banknote issuance, and foreign trade in 1939. It also includes a Yokohama consular memorandum on the importation of discounted yen and a Kobe consular report on Japan’s gold situation, with supporting clippings and statistical attachments.

subfiles.title: 1939 Gold Exports by Months
subfiles.about: Lists monthly gold exports through June 10, 1939.
subfiles.summary: Continuation of an earlier attachment tabulating gold shipments declared at Osaka and Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Attachment No. 2 cover
subfiles.about: Introduces a summary of gold exports of unstated origin.
subfiles.summary: Cover for Attachment No. 2.

subfiles.title: Gold Exports of Origin Not Named in Government Statements
subfiles.about: Compares 1937–1939 gold exports with bank reserve withdrawals and reported purchases.
subfiles.summary: Calculates 122,565.88 kilograms of exports whose gold source was unstated.

subfiles.title: Attachment No. 3 cover
subfiles.about: Introduces extracts of the finance minister’s remarks.
subfiles.summary: Cover for Attachment No. 3.

subfiles.title: Finance Minister’s Remarks on Gold, Notes and Bonds
subfiles.about: Ishiwata discusses North China currency, government bonds, and Japan’s gold supply.
subfiles.summary: Ishiwata calls the Federal Reserve Bank note’s weakness temporary, rejects compulsory bond purchases, denies an imminent loss of specie reserves, and declines to raise the official gold buying price.

subfiles.title: Comments of Minister of Finance on Gold
subfiles.about: A roundtable debates releasing specie reserves during the war.
subfiles.summary: Murata links costly shipping and commodity prices to restrictions intended to prevent gold outflow; Tsuda urges gold mining. Ishiwata says a protracted war limits the government’s ability to release gold.

subfiles.title: Attachment No. 4 cover: Compulsory Gold Census
subfiles.about: Introduces material on the compulsory gold census.
subfiles.summary: Cover for Attachment No. 4.

subfiles.title: 1939 Compulsory Gold Census
subfiles.about: Describes required registration of privately owned gold articles in July 1939.
subfiles.summary: Households and organizations must report most gold possessions from July 1 to 5; listed necessities are exempt, and false reporting risks a fine.

subfiles.title: Attachment No. 5 cover: Gold Mining Encouragement
subfiles.about: Introduces gold mining policy extracts.
subfiles.summary: Cover for Attachment No. 5.

subfiles.title: Encouragement to Alluvial Gold Mining
subfiles.about: Explains revised subsidies and indemnities for alluvial prospecting and refinery construction.
subfiles.summary: Revisions extend public support to alluvial prospecting and lower grade ore refining. The government will indemnify losses incurred by the promotion company on ordered advances and subsidies.

subfiles.title: Gold Smelter Construction
subfiles.about: Reports a plan to build smelters for lower grade ore.
subfiles.summary: Three of ten planned smelters are to be built in 1939, including one at Higoroichi.

subfiles.title: Fund Ready to Aid Gold
subfiles.about: Reports planned government spending to encourage gold production.
subfiles.summary: A finance official estimates ¥28 million in 1939–40 assistance for prospecting, technicians, and related work.

subfiles.title: Revisions to Gold Fund Special Account Law and Gold Production Law
subfiles.about: Summarizes new investment powers and compulsory gold purchase authority.
subfiles.summary: The revisions broaden permitted Gold Fund investments and authorize restrictions on gold disposal and compulsory sales.

subfiles.title: Attachment No. 6 cover: Banknote Expansion
subfiles.about: Introduces material on fiduciary note issuance.
subfiles.summary: Cover for Attachment No. 6.

subfiles.title: Fiduciary Note Issue Expansion
subfiles.about: Explains higher fiduciary note limits for three banks.
subfiles.summary: The 1939 laws raise note issue limits for the banks of Japan, Chosen, and Taiwan amid increased demand for currency.

subfiles.title: Bank of Japan Notes
subfiles.about: Outlines Bank of Japan note issue rules and reserve requirements.
subfiles.summary: Describes the bank’s authority to issue notes against reserves and securities, including the 1939 rise in its fiduciary limit.

subfiles.title: Bank of Japan Notes in Circulation
subfiles.from: The Oriental Economist; The Japan Times
subfiles.about: Lists selected annual and monthly totals of Bank of Japan notes in circulation.
subfiles.summary: Tabulates note circulation for 1936–1939.

subfiles.title: Attachment No. 7 cover: International Payments
subfiles.about: Introduces articles on Japan’s international payments.
subfiles.summary: Cover for Attachment No. 7.

subfiles.title: International Payments Since 1937
subfiles.about: Estimates Japan’s international payment balances despite unpublished official figures.
subfiles.summary: The article estimates a 1938 deficit of roughly ¥500 million and expects another, smaller debit balance in 1939. It discusses gold shipments, trade with Manchukuo and China, and Osaka bonds redeemed in London.

subfiles.title: Expansion of Export Loan System
subfiles.about: Advocates wider export credit for exporters and manufacturers.
subfiles.summary: The editorial credits government indemnities with expanding bank loans to smaller exporters and describes revised eligibility and documentation rules. It urges similar support for manufacturers of export goods.

subfiles.title: Attachment No. 8 cover: Excess of Imports
subfiles.about: Introduces a 1939 trade table.
subfiles.summary: Cover for Attachment No. 8.

subfiles.title: Japan’s Excess of Imports over Exports, January–April 1939
subfiles.about: Calculates imports and exports inside and outside the yen bloc.
subfiles.summary: Shows an overall import excess of ¥73.1 million and an import excess outside the yen bloc of ¥260.1 million.

subfiles.title: Consular Cover Letter on Importation of Yen
subfiles.about: Forwards Vice Consul White’s memorandum on yen imported into Yokohama.
subfiles.summary: Boyce sends a confidential memorandum based on banking, official, shipping, and business sources.

subfiles.title: Importation of “Cheap” Yen into Yokohama
subfiles.about: Examines discounted yen imports and their effect on Japan’s foreign exchange receipts.
subfiles.summary: White describes how seamen, tourists, returning emigrants, charities, and foreign residents acquired discounted yen abroad, reducing foreign currency spent in Japan. He also reports illicit exchange dealing, export undervaluation, and official restrictions introduced in 1939. He concludes that the rules may curb legal imports while Shanghai’s rates still encourage smuggling.

subfiles.title: Telegram on Bar Gold Shipment
subfiles.about: Reports an imminent gold shipment to San Francisco.
subfiles.summary: Reports 10,892.327 troy ounces of bar gold valued at ¥1,608,901.80 and asks that Treasury be informed.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Note on Japan’s Gold Situation
subfiles.about: Summarizes the Kobe consul’s report on gold exports, production, and reserves.
subfiles.summary: Notes ¥1.9 billion in shipments since 1937, weak gold production, and the sale of the last foreign gold mining concession. It suggests privately held gold or bank reserves may be helping sustain exports.

subfiles.title: Japan’s Gold Situation cover
subfiles.about: Identifies a confidential Kobe consular report.
subfiles.summary: Cover names the author, subject, and completion and mailing dates.

subfiles.title: Japan’s Gold Situation table of contents
subfiles.about: Lists topics covered by the consular report.
subfiles.summary: Indexes sections on gold exports, mining, the Unsan sale, gold censuses, and trade.

subfiles.title: Japan’s Gold Situation index of enclosures
subfiles.about: Lists the report’s statistical and press attachments.
subfiles.summary: Indexes seven numbered attachments and their subdivisions.

subfiles.title: Japan’s Gold Situation
subfiles.from: L. H. Gourley, American Consul at Kobe
subfiles.about: Assesses whether Japan can sustain gold exports amid weak production and foreign payment needs.
subfiles.summary: Gourley calculates that gold shipments to the United States since March 1937 reached 483.74 metric tons, worth ¥1.9 billion, while reported bank reserves remained unchanged in 1939. He cites labor and finance problems in gold mining, details the sale of the American Unsan concession, and surveys proposed new extraction methods and mint capacity. He suggests purchases of privately held gold helped sustain exports and notes that imports outside the yen bloc exceeded exports.

subfiles.title: Attachment No. 1 cover: Gold Exports
subfiles.about: Introduces gold export tables.
subfiles.summary: Cover for Attachment No. 1.

subfiles.title: Gold Exports from Japan in 1937, 1938 and 1939
subfiles.about: Totals Japanese gold exports through September 1939.
subfiles.summary: Records 483.74 metric tons of gold exports valued at ¥1.904 billion.

subfiles.title: 1939 Gold Shipments to United States by Months
subfiles.about: Itemizes declared shipments from January through September.
subfiles.summary: Lists shipment dates, weights, and values; nine-month exports total 88.43 metric tons and ¥366.32 million.

subfiles.title: Attachment No. 2 cover: Increased Gold Production
subfiles.about: Introduces press extracts on gold production.
subfiles.summary: Cover for Attachment No. 2.

subfiles.title: Need of Increased Gold Production
subfiles.from: The Japan Advertiser; The Japan Times; The Japan Chronicle
subfiles.about: Reports official pressure to increase gold output and debates obstacles.
subfiles.summary: Articles describe poor first-half production, labor shortages, snow damage, and financing difficulties. Officials order higher output and discuss reopening mines, building refineries, reducing freight rates, and recruiting Korean, Chinese, and juvenile workers.

subfiles.title: Attachment No. 3 cover: American Gold Concession
subfiles.about: Introduces clippings on the Unsan mine sale.
subfiles.summary: Cover for Attachment No. 3.

subfiles.title: Sale of American Gold Concession in Chosen
subfiles.about: Reports the proposed sale of Oriental Consolidated’s Unsan concession.
subfiles.summary: The article examines share prices, payment terms, exchange controls, and plans by the Japanese buyer to expand production. It also recounts the concession’s history and the rising cost of mining its deeper workings.

subfiles.title: Chosen Gold
subfiles.about: Recounts the history and sale of the American gold concession in Korea.
subfiles.summary: Time traces the concession’s origins, ownership, dividends, and Japan’s restrictions on gold sales. It reports the $8,174,500 sale to Nippon Mining and the installment payment guarantee.

subfiles.title: Gold Mining in Korea
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese purchase of the Unsan mine.
subfiles.summary: The clipping says exchange control issues were resolved and estimates a five-year installment price near ¥25 million.

subfiles.title: Gold Mine in Korea Sold by Americans
subfiles.about: Reports the end of American gold mine operations in Korea.
subfiles.summary: Reports the Unsan purchase and says exchange control had delayed the agreement.

subfiles.title: Attachment No. 4 cover: New Methods of Getting Gold
subfiles.about: Introduces clippings on proposed gold extraction methods.
subfiles.summary: Cover for Attachment No. 4.

subfiles.title: Gold from Seabed off Korean Coast
subfiles.from: The Japan Advertiser; The Japan Times
subfiles.about: Describes proposed seabed gold mining near Mokpo.
subfiles.summary: Two articles report promising test prospecting and plans to drain and dredge coastal seabed using embankments and pumps. Masatoshi Okochi’s company hopes to begin work near Mokpo and later use reclaimed land for cotton.

subfiles.title: Gold Sifter Invention
subfiles.about: Describes Kimura’s proposed machine for recovering gold from poor deposits.
subfiles.summary: Finance Ministry experts inspect a pump and hose sifter, with a field demonstration planned on the Kuji River.

subfiles.title: Attachment No. 5 cover: Tokyo Branch Mint
subfiles.about: Introduces a clipping on the Tokyo branch mint.
subfiles.summary: Cover for Attachment No. 5.

subfiles.title: Tokyo Branch Mint
subfiles.about: Reports completion of a Tokyo branch of the Osaka Mint.
subfiles.summary: The new branch will refine eastern Japan’s gold using two electric and three gas furnaces.

subfiles.title: Attachment No. 6 cover: Official Gold Price
subfiles.about: Introduces gold price articles and tables.
subfiles.summary: Cover for Attachment No. 6.

subfiles.title: Gold Price
subfiles.from: The Japan Chronicle; The Oriental Economist
subfiles.about: Discusses the official gold buying price and lists historical prices.
subfiles.summary: Authorities say they do not plan to raise the official price despite a widening gap with international values. Tables list government buying prices from 1932 to 1938 and Tokyo market averages through July 1939.

subfiles.title: Attachment No. 7 cover: Excess of Imports
subfiles.about: Introduces the January–June 1939 trade table.
subfiles.summary: Cover for Attachment No. 7.

subfiles.title: Japan’s Excess of Imports over Exports, January–June 1939
subfiles.about: Compares total trade with trade outside the yen bloc.
subfiles.summary: Shows an overall import excess of ¥23.9 million and an import excess outside the yen bloc of ¥409.6 million.

subfiles.title: Department of State Charge Slip
subfiles.about: Records a file charge for document 894.515/364.
subfiles.summary: Administrative charge slip bearing the name Costrell.
